title: Wildfire
protagonist: Response Commander Rex Dobson, National Interagency Fire Center
primary_metric: hours of lead time before the fire, at its currently reported flank rate of spread, reaches each town's outskirts

options.A: Recommend the National Guard rapid response force be deployed to San Fernando
options.B: Recommend the National Guard rapid response force be deployed to Santa Clarita

new_coverage_note: Legacy-conversion case. Checked every claimed skill's spine 'n' count directly (readmodel/standards_spine.json) rather than assuming: all 15 skills claimed here already have n>0 (prior case coverage exists), so new_coverage[] is genuinely empty. The original legacy tagging listed Wildfire against 91 spine skills (essentially the entire basic-operations/number-sense/geometry/measurement/statistics surface) -- almost none of which any Challenge-3 deliverable actually forces. This conversion cut that list to the 15 skills the case's own five deliverables (D1-D5) genuinely require, per the LEARNING GOAL CHECK (see LEARNING_GOALS.md), rather than padding standards[] to manufacture a non-empty new_coverage[]. No skill with n==0 in the current spine near this case's actual T3 MS-stretch level (rate-of-spread/area/proportion arithmetic) was found to be genuinely forced by any deliverable -- the two n==0 skills nearest this topic (pre-calculus unit circle, calculus instantaneous rate of change) are above this case's tier and not something any deliverable requires.
legacy_conversion_note: Original source (source/Y3/Session 3/Wildfire/Case Study_ Wildfire.docx, Guide Notes.docx, and a fire-perimeter reference PDF) is a fictional wildfire scenario (the 'Soledad Canyon Fire') overlaid on real Southern California geography -- Agua Dulce, Santa Clarita, San Fernando, and Solemint are real places, and the rate-of-spread figures (35 chains/hour southern head, 27 chains/hour southwestern flank), slope percentages, and wind speeds are the legacy case's own given scenario data, preserved verbatim as stated field reports (not independently sourceable, since the fire itself is fictional -- these are treated the same way Cardiology treated its disclosed cost-modeling convention, not as claims requiring an external citation). What WAS independently verified and updated: (1) the chain-to-feet and chain-to-acre unit conversions, sourced fresh from NWCG's own Firefighter Math course (the same real training-course family the legacy case's own Appendix D already linked to); (2) real 2020/2024 Census population, land-area, and household-size figures for Santa Clarita, San Fernando, and Agua Dulce, replacing the legacy case's total absence of usable town-scale data; (3) real route-distance figures from Agua Dulce to each town. The legacy case's own D1/D2 questions ('how many acres by 23:59 tonight,' 'how many people lose their homes today') had no baseline fire-size or population-density data behind them at all in the original -- a genuine gap in the 2021 source, not a number that drifted. Rather than inventing baseline acreage or population figures to fill that gap (which SPEC.md Sec.5 and MCS-21 forbid), this conversion redesigned D1 as an explicit upper-bound sector-growth model (Modeling Assumption MA1, using the real ~45-degree compass angle between the fire's own two reported bearings) and D2 as an explicit density-proxy model (MA2, using Agua Dulce's own real, cited Census housing density) -- both disclosed as stated modeling conventions, not claims of precise real-world prediction. The legacy Overview's '85% of all structures in Agua Dulce were destroyed' figure was cut from the Overview (SPEC Sec.1.2 forbids load-bearing numbers there) and is not reintroduced as a deliverable input anywhere, since no deliverable needs it -- it was decorative in the original. Computing D3/D4 (time-to-town at each flank's reported rate) against the real route distances surfaced a finding the legacy case's own framing did not anticipate: at the reported 05:00 rates, BOTH towns are more than two days away, not hours -- meaning the legacy prompt's 'by 23:59 tonight' urgency framing does not actually hold for the town-arrival question, only for the immediate-vicinity acreage/structure-loss question (D1/D2). This became this conversion's authored Twist (see FACILITATOR.md) rather than being smoothed over.

modeling_assumptions.text: D1's anticipated acreage is modeled as a 45-degree sector (the real compass angle between due-south, the reported head bearing, and due-southwest, the reported flank bearing) grown from a point at the higher reported rate (35 chains/hour, southern head), held constant from 05:00 to 23:59 (18h59m).
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Acreage scales with the square of elapsed time and linearly with the sector angle -- an earlier check-in time or a narrower/wider confirmed wedge both move the estimate sharply.

modeling_assumptions.text: D2 applies Agua Dulce CDP's real 2020 Census housing density, occupancy rate, and household size to D1's acreage, as a proxy for structures/people newly at risk tonight, since the newly-threatened ground is the same rural/exurban corridor Agua Dulce sits in.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: If the true density of the newly-threatened ground is lower (more undeveloped wildland), D2 is a real overestimate -- it is disclosed as an upper bound, not a forecast.

modeling_assumptions.text: The fire's current position, for distance purposes, is modeled at Agua Dulce -- the last confirmed location it reached.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: If the fire's true leading edge is already past Agua Dulce toward one town, that town's D3/D4 arrival time shrinks.

modeling_assumptions.text: Real driving-route mileage (Appendix C) is used as the distance the fire must cover to reach each town, rather than straight-line distance, because Santa Ana wind-driven fire in this terrain tends to run along canyon/ridge corridors roughly paralleling the road network.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Switching to straight-line distance would shorten both D3 and D4 by a similar proportion -- check whether the margin survives the switch (this is exactly what sensitivity_model.py's FLEX sweep tests). It does not: the real, re-verified margin is only 1.1% (2026-08-13 correction; see balance.stability), and the FLEX sweep shows it flipping the A/B winner well before a straight-line-distance-sized change, let alone the full +/-50% swing.

modeling_assumptions.text: Each flank's 05:00 rate of spread is held constant for the full period modeled in D1-D4, rather than adjusted for Appendix A's forecast (which shows wind climbing sharply after 11:00).
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: If real fire behavior accelerates with the forecast wind increase, both D1's acreage and D3/D4's arrival times are underestimates of the true danger -- the real threat likely arrives sooner than this model says.

deliverables.text: Acres NIFC should anticipate burning between 05:00 and 23:59 tonight, modeled as a 45-degree sector grown at the higher reported rate of spread (Appendix D, MA1).
How many people NIFC should expect to lose their homes today, using D1's acreage and Agua Dulce's real structure-density figures (Appendix C, MA2).
If Option A: how long, at the current reported rate, the fire would take to reach San Fernando, and what location at its edge the rapid response team should defend.
If Option B: how long, at the current reported rate, the fire would take to reach Santa Clarita, and what location at its edge the rapid response team should defend.
A recommendation for Commander Dobson, weighing D3/D4's lead time against the populations at stake (Appendix C).

balance.argument_a: San Fernando is the smaller, denser town by land area (2.37 sq mi vs. Santa Clarita's 70.75 sq mi), so a fire line failure there concentrates damage in a tight urban footprint. Its raw lead-time case is no longer strong: at the reported southern-head ROS (35 ch/hr = 0.4375 mph) and the real, re-verified 25.3-mile route distance, the fire reaches its outskirts in about 57.8 hours -- now the *longer*, not shorter, of the two lead times (see 2026-08-13 sensitivity re-check below).
balance.argument_b: Santa Clarita is the higher-stakes option on population, and after the 2026-08-13 re-verification of both route distances it is also now the marginally shorter-fuse option: at the reported southwestern-flank ROS (27 ch/hr = 0.3375 mph) and the real, re-verified 19.3-mile route distance, the fire reaches its outskirts in about 57.2 hours -- about 0.6 hours (1.1%) sooner than San Fernando. Santa Clarita's population (228,673) is about 9.6 times San Fernando's (23,946), so a failed fire line there costs vastly more, and it no longer trades that against a real lead-time disadvantage.
balance.margin_basis: Primary metric is lead time in hours before each town's outskirts is reached, at that flank's own reported rate of spread, over the real route distance from the fire's modeled position at Agua Dulce (MA3/MA4). San Fernando: 25.3 mi / 0.4375 mph = 57.829h. Santa Clarita: 19.3 mi / 0.3375 mph = 57.185h. Margin = (57.829 - 57.185) / 57.829 = 1.1%.
balance.stability: 2026-08-13 Tier 2 probe 5 re-check, per MCS-26/MCS-41 (no disclosure-aware pass state -- see DOCTRINE_LEDGER.md): a genuine retune was attempted first, not skipped. The original 24mi/23mi figures were re-verified against live Google Maps routing (see sources[] S5/S5b) rather than re-used from memory, and the real current values (25.3mi to San Fernando, 19.3mi to Santa Clarita) turned out to be MORE lopsided in ratio than the stale figures, not less -- and they flip which option has the shorter lead time (Santa Clarita, not San Fernando, now arrives first, by ~0.6h/1.1%). This is not an authoring error to fix; both distances are now correctly sourced and the case's true lead-time margin genuinely is this thin. Because the honest margin is ~1.1%, sensitivity_model.py's mechanical +/-50% flex on dist_to_san_fernando_mi and dist_to_santa_clarita_mi flips the A/B winner in both directions (see FLEX sweep output) -- elimination is not honestly available here; the instability is real and is disclosed here and in FACILITATOR.md Lessons Learned rather than hidden. Per MCS-26/MCS-41, a disclosed-but-not-eliminated instability is a permanent P5 FAIL, not a pass -- recorded as such in qa.tier2.P5 below.

derived._note: Computed during conversion from Appendix C/D's given and cited data; case-readiness should re-derive independently. See sensitivity_model.py for the runnable version.

sensitivity_note: This case models real people losing real homes in a fast-moving disaster, framed around protection (which town's fire line to defend) rather than casualty optimization, consistent with SPEC.md Sec.6. Facilitators should keep the discussion on the real geography/census math and the case's own disclosed modeling assumptions, not on personal wildfire-evacuation experiences from the room, which can turn a math discussion into something a facilitator isn't equipped to hold.
